title: How many Indigenous people were enslaved in the Americas between 1492 and 1900?
short: Andrés Reséndez's estimate of 2.5 to 5 million enslaved Indigenous people is the only hemispheric figure, and it rests on regional extrapolation rather than a count.
matters: The scale of Indigenous enslavement determines how far the demographic collapse of the Americas should be attributed to coerced labor, displacement and violence rather than to epidemic disease alone. It affects the comparison between Indigenous and African slavery in the colonial economies of the Caribbean, Brazil, Chile, northern Mexico, the American Southwest and the English colonies of the Southeast and New England. It also bears on how historians read Spanish and Portuguese abolitions of Indian slavery (1542, 1570, 1755) that were repeatedly evaded through categories such as just war, rescate, encomienda, peonage and 'adoption'.
stuck: Indigenous slavery was frequently illegal or ambiguously legal, so it was recorded under euphemisms (criados, piezas, naborías, administrados, captives) or not recorded at all, and it was dispersed across many small transactions rather than concentrated in shipping. The surviving evidence is scattered among notarial protocols, lawsuits, baptismal registers, probate inventories, military reports and Indigenous testimony in Spanish, Portuguese, French, English and Indigenous languages, mostly undigitized or uncatalogued at item level. Reséndez's 2.5–5 million figure, which he presents as a cautious range, therefore aggregates regional estimates of very different quality, and several regions (Amazonia, the Río de la Plata, Central America after 1550) have no systematic count.
solved: A published, source-linked database of individual enslaved Indigenous people and enslaving events, organized by region and period, from which documented minimums can be computed and combined with explicit, testable multipliers for under-recording, producing a hemispheric range that others can recompute region by region.
approach: AI agents could read digitized notarial protocols, baptismal and burial registers, freedom suits and probate inventories, flag every person described by terms associated with Indigenous bondage, and link repeated appearances of the same individual across record types for historians to review.

The main obstacle is access: progress depends on digitizing and indexing notarial and judicial series in Seville, Mexico City, Santiago de Chile, São Paulo, Lima and Santa Fe in partnership with those archives, and on working with Indigenous communities and projects such as Native Bound Unbound that are already assembling records.

existing.title: Indian Slavery in Colonial Times within the Present Limits of the United States
existing.venue: New York: Columbia University (Studies in History, Economics and Public Law)
existing.note: First survey of Indigenous enslavement in the English, French and Spanish colonies north of Mexico.

existing.title: Indian Slavery and the Cerrato Reforms
existing.note: Showed the scale of Indian slavery in Guatemala and the effects of the New Laws' enforcement in the 1540s.

existing.title: Indian Labor and New World Plantations: European Demands and Indian Responses in Northeastern Brazil
existing.note: Documented the reliance of early Bahian sugar plantations on enslaved and coerced Indigenous labor before the transition to African slavery.

existing.title: Forced Native Labor in Sixteenth-Century Central America
existing.note: Regional study including the export of enslaved Indigenous people from Nicaragua and Honduras to Panama and Peru.

existing.title: From Indian to Slave: Forced Native Labour and Colonial Society in São Paulo during the Seventeenth Century
existing.note: Used São Paulo probate inventories to show the scale of bandeirante enslavement; expanded in Negros da terra (1994).

existing.title: The Indian Slave Trade: The Rise of the English Empire in the American South, 1670–1717
existing.note: Argued that between roughly 24,000 and 51,000 Indigenous people were captured and sold through the Carolina trade between 1670 and 1715, many of them exported to the Caribbean.

existing.title: Captives and Cousins: Slavery, Kinship, and Community in the Southwest Borderlands
existing.venue: Chapel Hill: Omohundro Institute / University of North Carolina Press
existing.note: Used New Mexico baptismal registers and legal records to trace captive exchange among Spanish, Pueblo, Navajo, Apache and Comanche communities into the nineteenth century.

existing.title: Indigenous Slavery in South America, 1492–1820
existing.venue: In David Eltis and Stanley L. Engerman (eds.), The Cambridge World History of Slavery, vol. 3 (Cambridge University Press), 248–272
existing.note: Continental synthesis covering both Indigenous and European-driven slaving in South America.

existing.title: Bonds of Alliance: Indigenous and Atlantic Slaveries in New France
existing.venue: Chapel Hill: Omohundro Institute / University of North Carolina Press
existing.note: Reconstructed thousands of enslaved Indigenous people (panis) in French colonial records from the Great Lakes to the Caribbean.

existing.title: Global Indios: The Indigenous Struggle for Justice in Sixteenth-Century Spain
existing.note: Analyzes more than one hundred freedom suits brought in Castile between 1530 and 1585 by enslaved Indigenous people transported to Iberia.

existing.title: Brethren by Nature: New England Indians, Colonists, and the Origins of American Slavery
existing.note: Shows the centrality of Indigenous enslavement and export in New England, especially after the Pequot War and King Philip's War.

existing.title: The Other Slavery: The Uncovered Story of Indian Enslavement in America
existing.note: Hemispheric synthesis proposing that between 2.5 and 5 million Indigenous people were enslaved from 1492 to 1900, excluding encomienda and repartimiento labor.

existing.authors: Arne Bialuschewski and Linford D. Fisher
existing.title: Guest Editors' Introduction: New Directions in the History of Native American Slavery Studies
existing.note: Introduces a special issue on seventeenth-century Indigenous slavery and surveys the hemispheric literature in several languages.

archives.collection: Justicia and Escribanía de Cámara (freedom suits of indios esclavos, 1530s–1580s); Patronato; Audiencia de Chile and Audiencia de Guatemala correspondence
archives.note: Lawsuits and royal inquiries naming enslaved Indigenous people; many legajos imaged on PARES but not described at the level of individuals.

holdings.name: Justicia
holdings.note: Sixteenth-century lawsuits and residencias, including freedom suits of Indigenous people held as slaves.

holdings.name: Escribanía de Cámara de Justicia
holdings.note: Appeals and suits heard by the Council of the Indies, a second series in which freedom suits and complaints about enslavement may appear.

holdings.name: Audiencia de Guatemala
holdings.note: Correspondence and expedientes of the audiencia, relevant to enslavement in Central America.

holdings.name: Audiencia de Chile
holdings.note: Letters and expedientes of the president and oidores of Chile to the Council of the Indies, including reports on the war and on enslavement of Mapuche prisoners.

archives.repository: Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City
archives.collection: Ramos Indios, Inquisición, Provincias Internas, Civil and Tierras
archives.note: Records of captives taken in the Chichimeca and northern frontier wars and of freedom petitions; indexed mostly through printed AGN catalogues.

holdings.name: Fondo Hospital de Jesús
holdings.note: Papers of the Hospital de Jesús, 1520 to 1925, including labour and servile status of workers on the Cortés estates.

archives.repository: Archivo Nacional Histórico, Santiago de Chile
archives.collection: Real Audiencia, Capitanía General and Escribanos de Santiago (sales and registrations of Mapuche captives, 1608–1683 and after)
archives.note: Notarial and judicial evidence for the legal enslavement of Mapuche prisoners of war under the 1608 royal decree.

holdings.name: Escribanos de Santiago
holdings.note: Notarial protocols of Santiago, 1559 to 1800 (973 volumes), the main source for sales and deposits of captives; described in the ANH synoptic table of fondos.

holdings.name: Real Audiencia
holdings.note: Court records of the Audiencia of Santiago, 1600 to 1830 (3,254 volumes), including litigation over captives.

holdings.name: Capitanía General
holdings.note: Governors' papers, 1597 to 1823, relevant to the Mapuche frontier.

archives.repository: Arquivo Público do Estado de São Paulo
archives.collection: Inventários e Testamentos (probate inventories of the seventeenth century, partly published in a printed series from 1920)
archives.note: Inventories listing Indigenous 'administrados' and 'negros da terra' held by bandeirante households; the basis of Monteiro's estimates.

holdings.name: Inventários e Testamentos
holdings.note: Published transcriptions of São Paulo probate inventories and wills, volume 1 issued in 1920; scans of volumes 1 to 31 are on the Internet Archive.

archives.repository: New Mexico State Records Center and Archives, Santa Fe
archives.collection: Spanish Archives of New Mexico I and II; Mexican Archives of New Mexico
archives.note: Colonial and Mexican-period government records documenting captives and genízaros; microfilm editions exist, with church registers held separately by the Archdiocese of Santa Fe.

holdings.name: Spanish Archives of New Mexico II (SANM II)
holdings.note: Spanish colonial administrative, civil, military and ecclesiastical records, 1621 to 1821; the originals are in Santa Fe and the University of New Mexico holds microfilm.

archives.repository: South Carolina Department of Archives and History, Columbia
archives.collection: Journals of the Commissioners of the Indian Trade; Records of the Secretary of the Province (bills of sale)
archives.note: Evidence for the Carolina trade in Indigenous captives, c. 1670–1720.

holdings.name: Journals of the Commissioners of the Indian Trade, 1710-1718
holdings.note: The Commissioners' manuscript journals as published by the Archives Department in 1955 (ed. W. L. McDowell); they record purchases and trade in Indigenous captives.

archives.repository: Native Bound Unbound (Mellon Foundation-funded digital project)
archives.collection: Digital repository of records of Indigenous captivity and slavery across the Americas (legal cases, censuses, wills, church registers, objects)
archives.note: Assembling person-level records and transcriptions from archives in several countries; the nearest existing equivalent to a hemispheric database.
